stem:
A 7-year-old presents with recurrent episodes of wheeze and nocturnal cough.

How should asthma be diagnosed at this age?

options.label: A
options.text: Spirometry showing FEV1 improvement ≥12% OR FeNO ≥25 ppb
options.explanation:
Correct. In a 7-year-old, asthma diagnosis is supported by objective testing such as spirometric reversibility or an elevated FeNO.

Children use the same ≥12% FEV1 reversibility threshold as adults — the paediatric difference is no absolute ≥200mL volume requirement, not a lower percentage.

options.label: B
options.text: Clinical diagnosis only — no testing possible at age ≤5 years
options.explanation: That approach applies to younger preschool children, not a 7-year-old. School-age children should usually have objective testing rather than a diagnosis based on symptoms alone.

options.label: C
options.text: Trial of salbutamol and clinical response ≥3 days
options.explanation: A bronchodilator trial is more useful in 1-5 year olds, where formal lung function testing is limited. At age 7, spirometry and FeNO are the more appropriate diagnostic tools.

options.label: D
options.text: Peak expiratory flow diary for ≥4 weeks
options.explanation: Peak flow diaries can support monitoring, but they are not the main recommended diagnostic test here. Objective confirmation in this age group usually relies on spirometry and/or FeNO.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Skin prick testing can identify atopy, but it does not diagnose asthma itself. A child can be allergic without having objective evidence of asthma.

context:
Asthma diagnosis depends on age: under 12 months it is not diagnosed (bronchiolitis); 1 to 5 years it is clinical, with response to a salbutamol trial; from about 6, when a child can perform spirometry, it is objective.

Objective evidence is reversible obstruction: FEV1 rising by 12% or more after salbutamol. FeNO (fractional exhaled nitric oxide) is a breath test for eosinophilic airway inflammation; 25 ppb or more in a child supports the diagnosis.

A normal FeNO does not exclude asthma (non-eosinophilic phenotypes), which is why spirometry stays the anchor.
